first.explanation: Mid-word fragment tokens that start a word split after "a/an/the": a separate token like "were" in werewolf, "is" in isomer/isle, "can" in canes/cancel, "makes" in makeshift, "was" in wasp.

Predicts structural continuation tokens: the newline after sign-offs/headers ("Thanks,", "Regards,", "Originally Posted by"), the comma after publisher names, and the ** or * operator in polynomial terms of derivative problems.

Blank-line break (double newline) after a completed statement or closing brace inside indented code, before the next statement/method begins; occasionally ' was'/' +' after a subject in prose or math.

retest.explanation: Blank-line break (double newline) after a completed statement or block in code, within an indented function body, right before the next logical section; also weakly fires on 'was'/'+' mid-sentence.

first.explanation: The infinitive 'to' (or auxiliary/linking verb) right after aspectual verbs like began/started/beginning/yet, predicting an upcoming change-of-state verb (e.g., 'began [to] fray', 'starts [to] brown').

The first token of an identifier/variable name (e.g. user, root, env, d, db) that repeats a name seen earlier in the context, typically after a comma or at line start in code, predicting its continuation like ->field or _suffix.
The word "as" (or a plural noun like women/mothers/nurses) right after a noun phrase, where it begins an adjunct such as "as well as", "as described", "as a function of", or a role complement.

Adverbs inserted right after a subject or a comma before a verb phrase, especially "thereby"/"thus" opening a consequence participle clause, also "often", "ultimately", "famously", predicting the upcoming verb or participle.

Predicts the next token in highly memorized boilerplate or formulaic text (legal headers, license text, constants, API calls, citations), firing on mid-phrase tokens like '(', '⏎', ' to', 'Klu[wer]', ' INCIDENT'.

Predicts the word right after a noun/copula that introduces an explanation, cause, or pro/con: 'due' (to), 'advantage/disadvantage' (of/that), 'is' (because/that), 'expense', 'case', or a colon introducing the explanation.

A proper name (person, company, element, or concept) that is used as a modifier or is the start of a name, often awaiting a suffix like -ian, -ism, or -Macaulay (Chev|ron, Cohen, Marx, Freud, Cu, Jesus).

Predicts a highly expected, formulaic next word in boilerplate text: legal phrases (found guilty, the court), 'first' adverbs, 'table'/'fig' ref-types, repeated 'sqrt' in math simplification, and formulaic 'I have hereunto'.

Connector token right after the first item/number in a list or operation (comma, 'and', 'or', '+', '-'), or an underscore/hyphen inside identifiers, where the next token is a second operand or word part.

Fires on the token after a subject/"if" in "if you/she/I want(s) to" (the verb 'want'), and on structural connectors in section-ID labels ({#sec3dot2-sensors}) or the digit '0' after 'Let c =' in decimals.

Short function-word or word-fragment tokens just before the rest of a word/phrase, especially French split tokens (to|i, all|ons, a|vez, n|'), plus 'nothing/more to', 'before' (court), and case-number digits.
The preposition "between" (or French "entre") right after words like difference, differ, vary, or significant, introducing the compared groups; also "into"/"to" after randomized/assigned into groups.

Sentence-ending periods (mostly in informal forum or opinion prose) that complete a declarative statement, just before a new sentence or paragraph begins; also fires weakly on mid-clause function words such as 'is', 'are', and 't.

Function tokens that open a clause or parenthetical after a noun/verb: dashes (– — -) setting off appositives or asides, and "that"/"for"/"with" after requires/need/imperative; also French "laiss-" fragments.

Adjective/adverb or quantity word inside a degree or comparison construction, especially after "how" (how important), plus "than", "as" (as far as), "enough", "ample", predicting the following complement clause.
The verb "let" (also make, put, keep) right after "to"/"and"/subject, predicting a pronoun object next (let her/him/me go). Weaker on mid-word fragments in names and foreign text.

Mid-token fragments inside URLs, phone numbers, version strings, and command-line flags, especially the "2" in LICENSE-2.0 and RSS 2.0, plus numeric URL pieces, hyphen flags, and word-stem pieces in non-English text.

The final token completing a hyphenated compound modifier inside a descriptive adjective list (e.g. "wood-panelled", "middle-aged", "state-of-the-art"), or the closing parenthesis of a parenthetical adjective, just before the noun.

Mid-word or function-word tokens that predict a specific continuation: word-start fragments like 'Dis'/'Ex'/'El', London postcode digits 'W1', map grid refs, 'close/closed/open', and infinitive 'to' after a subject.

The demonstrative or determiner ("that", "this", "the", "one") right after the preposition "at", especially in time phrases like "at that moment/point/time" at sentence start, and also locations like "at the University".

Tokens right after a time-span quantity (two weeks, several hours, ten years) predicting 'ago/later/old'; also paragraph-break newlines before numbered sections in legal opinions, and function words (of, in, for) in math/prose.

Predicts a continuation in patent/academic boilerplate: the word after phrases like 'directed', 'object of the invention', 'various/different/two/other' ("types"), 'there is' ("provided"), plus patent-number digit fragments and citation endings.

Function words that follow a subject or opener and precede a predicate, especially auxiliary 'do/did/does' in questions or negations, 'of' after 'part/half', plus table divider dashes, percent signs, and 'No.' case numbers.

Predicts a highly formulaic next word in guidebook/lab-methods prose: after "the [world]", "was [used/made/built]", city-comma-[Country] in supplier citations, paragraph-ending newlines, "By the [way]". Fires on tokens preceding stock continuations.

Sentence-initial or post-verb pronoun "It" (esp. after "figured"/"figure"), plus "thank [you]", "There [are/was]", and word fragments like "gour[met]", where the next token is a predictable continuation.

Verb or particle right after an existential 'there' or in list-introducing phrases ('there are/is also/will be/have been', 'others include', 'as shown by'), predicting an enumerated or additional item to follow.

retest.explanation: Verb or particle right after an existential 'there' or list-introducing phrase (there are/also/be; 'others include'; 'shown by'), where an enumerated item or new entity is about to be introduced.

first.explanation: Predicts a continuation after a subject/preposition where a verb complement or duration follows: mainly "want" in "I want to" (also German/Swedish modals like vill/ten), and duration numbers after "for" (30 min).
Newline token right after a short section heading (before a markdown ---/=== underline) or after a Q&A answer line; also causative verbs like 'made/leading' after a noun subject.

Punctuation/subword tokens right after an opening context where text is structured: opening quotes or brackets in code/dialogue, and words like 'departure', 'contributor', 'LIMITED' (BUT NOT LIMITED), predicting the next continuation.

The token right after a defined symbol or abbreviation, where its definition is about to begin: a separator (comma, colon, =) in abbreviation lists, or a verb/article like 'is the', 'denotes' after a variable in 'where X is…'.
The word "for" starting a loop statement at the beginning of a code line (also "for" ending "Solve ... for x"), and "of" in the phrase "of course" after a comma or sentence start.

Function word right after a person/object noun or verb that predicts an upcoming infinitive or complement: 'to' after asked/forced/urge + person, 'need' after subject, possessive ’ before s, 'for'/'by' after ask/passers.

Predicts the verb/copula or continuation right after a subject noun like "The problem" or "The issue" (mostly "is"), plus similar mid-clause function words ("to", "would"), and question-ending newlines before "A:".

Mid-token punctuation in rigid formulaic strings: the period in "L.Ed.2d" legal citations (strongest), the slash in polynomial fractions like "n**7/6300", plus occasional mid-phrase tokens like "year", "for", "dollars".

Mid-word subword fragments in Spanish/French/Portuguese words (and 'at'/'if' + 'no/not' constructions) where the next token is a predictable word completion; e.g. 'tí-p-ica', 'jusqu-'-à', 'if not', 'at no'.
In synthetic math problems, fires on operator tokens that begin a new term or factor (leading minus after newline, " (-", "*(", "/("). Also on "so" after "not" ("not so often/much").
Function words (esp. "the" after "What is/are") predicting the next noun in synthetic math-problem questions; also "the" or "facts/record" in legal opinions, and "=\"@" in Android XML.

Function-word or fragment tokens whose continuation is highly predictable, especially acknowledgement phrases ('thank', 'grateful to', 'indebted to'), sentence-initial 'Due' (to), elisions like l', and word-piece starts across languages.

Function words/connectors right after a formulaic head word, predicting the standard continuation: 'motion for', 'represented as', 'Thank you very much', 'recommend that', 'something like', 'respectfully dissent', 'according to', 'various'.

Mid-word subword fragments inside words in non-English text (Turkish, Hungarian, Finnish, Czech), often a vowel-initial or y-/ğ- continuation after a prefix; also the hyphen in citation IDs like [@B78-viruses-12-.

Prepositions or connectors introducing a method, means, or reference ("via", "using", "as", "for" in "see X for details"), and also LaTeX display-math openers like "$$\" after a colon or "defined as".

Punctuation/operator tokens that open an argument or operand, mid-expression: open paren after a function/method name in code, ' $' or digits starting a dollar amount, and operators like ' -', '/(-' in algebra exercises.

Adverb/function words after a verb or copula that precede a continuation, like 'really', 'so', 'as', 'all', 'well' (as well, it's really, felt so, all right); also mid-word fragments like 'were'wolf, 'types'.

Predicts the continuation after a preposition following a verb phrase of manner/gesture ("looked at him [with] contempt", "nodded [in] salute"), and also LaTeX subscript/superscript tokens after \int, \sum, \mathbb{Z/C}, or sqrt.

Tokens inside a proper-name/title or qualified identifier where a specific continuation is predicted: publication names after 'at/by/in' ("The" Hill), case names (Gaines v. Ski), and separators like context[.], color[:], file[/].

Fires on the token right after a number/unit or noun where a scientific or technical continuation follows: decimal points in measurements (4.4, 2.5), superscript minus in units (cm^−1), phone-prefix '%', and capitalized abbreviation starts (T2, CPM, DME).

Passive-voice participle or verb right after an auxiliary (is/was/are/been), especially 'deemed' and 'considered', also 'provided', 'introduced', 'used', 'required', predicting an evaluative or procedural complement.

retest.explanation: Passive-voice past participle (or auxiliary) right after "is/are/was/were/been", especially "deemed", "considered", "provided", "introduced", "used", "required", predicting an evaluative or procedural complement.

first.explanation: Relative/complementizer words ("that", "which", "what") introducing a subordinate clause after a noun or verb, especially in legal prose; also newlines in code and mid-token pieces of hashes or DNA sequences.

Fires right after a subject or relative pronoun (we, I, which, who) on an adverb (really, specifically, closely) or on a mid-word verb stem fragment (recon-, constru-, observ-) where a verb continuation is expected.
Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is highly predictable, especially "the" after "told" (told the BBC/crowd), "den" in "van den Broek", contraction "n't" after did/doesn't, and mid-word fragments.

Sentence-initial 'what' (or 'that'/'who') after conjunctions like So/But/Then/Now starting a rhetorical question, plus indentation/whitespace tokens right after an opening bracket or paren in code lists/imports.

Tokens right before an expected object/continuation: the '=' after a declared variable in C/ObjC/Java code (pointer type declarations), ternary ':' and casts, plus news words like protests/outrage/supporters/crowd that take a following 'of/against/at' phrase.

Tokens where a following word piece is strongly predicted: the " re" prefix (redefine, rewire), "of/from" after nouns, colons in letter-count sets, periods after equations in math problems, and "2." in RSS 2.0.
Token right after "on the" in contrast/location idioms ("on the [same/other] hand", "On the other hand"), and the opening parenthesis after "Let x be" in synthetic math problems.

retest.explanation: Tokens right after "On the" in contrast/location phrases ("on the [same/other] hand") and the opening parenthesis after "Let x be" or "Is" in synthetic math problems, where a continuing expression is expected.

first.explanation: Tokens in the middle of a construct where a specific continuation is highly predictable: code syntax (':', '.', 'then', 'throw'), mid-word fragments of multi-token words (aspen, toluene, benzo, olefin), and conjunctions like 'and/or' joining paired adjectives.

Tokens like "I", "he", "we", "me", "she", "it" (and "guidelines") that start a new clause or are word-fragments, e.g. "I" in IPC/ILEC/IHT, "me" in "mexpp", "she" in "sheaves"; often a pronoun beginning a relative clause.

Fires at structural boundary tokens where a predictable continuation follows: blank-line gaps after closing braces in code, table separator dashes, and auxiliary 'do/does/did' or 'of' (part of, third of) in prose.

Mid-structure tokens in predictable formatted text: the 'else' after a closing brace in code, figure/table reference numbers, star-page markers (*123) in legal text, and mid-word fragments in names or words.

Mid-word or mid-phrase tokens where a specific continuation is highly predictable: speech tags like "dit" after a quote, "Señor/Hr." before "Presidente/formand", "-based", and adjectives/prepositions awaiting a noun. Multilingual.

retest.explanation: Mid-word or function-word tokens where the next token is a predictable continuation: speech-verb "dit" after a quote in French, "Señor/Hr." in parliamentary addresses, "based", and word fragments.

first.explanation: Predicts the next word after formulaic head nouns/verbs in patent and academic boilerplate, e.g. "The present invention [relates]", "patent No. X [issued]", "definition/construction/description [of]", "point was [to]", "remanded".

Predictable continuation tokens in formulaic text: legal dispositions (cert. denied, dismissed, reversed, S.Ct.), guidebook price/hours ranges (£x.50, 10am-), phone prefixes (800), and duration words (a year, five months).

Function word right after an introductory adverbial or discourse opener ("On the", "Just for", "As with", "compared to", "Then there", "for every x there"), predicting the clause's continuation like "there is/exists" or a comparison.

Fires on "have" after modal verbs (could/would have + participle) in counterfactual constructions, plus structural glue tokens like "dot" in section IDs (sec2dot1), "=" or ":" in URLs/LaTeX labels, and "@" before Twitter handles.

Tokens in the middle of a predictable pairing or repetition, where the next token completes a learned pattern: 'whether [or] not', 'either [or] both', 'spent his [whole/entire] life', 'a [wide] range', and repeated arguments in code or figure caption line breaks.

Predicts a highly determined next token mid-pattern: binary minus/plus operators in algebra problems, fixed idioms (spoilt for choice, without specific prior permission, Pliny the Elder), and split multi-byte Chinese/Japanese characters.

Abbreviation period after a reporter/state name in legal citations (Kan., Ala., Ga., Cal.), plus the first token of a multi-token proper name (San Diego, Air Force, Jet Propulsion, Qualcomm) in an organization or location.

Word-start fragments of proper names/capitalized tokens after a line break, quote, or category label (e.g. "Category:Ch"), plus mid-sentence conjunctions like "if", "as if", "though", "although", "because" introducing a clause.

retest.explanation: Fires on the start of a new word or name (first-subword fragments after a quote, newline, or 'Category:') and on clause-linking conjunctions like 'if', 'as if', 'though', 'although', 'because' that begin a subordinate clause.

first.explanation: Small connector tokens mid-pattern: the '/' in fractions within math exercises, ' to' in opening-hours ranges ('Mon-Thu, to 11pm Fri'), ' to'/' this' as object or function words, and ':' in timestamps.

retest.explanation: Connector tokens where a following continuation is predicted: division slash in math fractions (numerator/denominator), "to" in opening-hour ranges ("Mon-Thu, to 11pm Fri"), plus "to" in clauses, "this", and time colons.

first.explanation: Mid-phrase word after a verb/modal/idiom where a particle or adverb completes it (could [just], think [twice], in [turn], in what [way], live [up], whether [or]); also partial-word tokens in non-English text.

Predicts the next token after a function-like connective in formulaic text: the multiplication '*' in synthetic algebra problems (e.g. 'Suppose 4*x'), '<' in p-values, and verbs like 'agree/confirm/provide' after 'These results'.

Fires on a token right after which a continuation is highly constrained: the 're' prefix before a verb stem (rethink, redefine), dialogue-turn closing quotes, 'Uh' in 'uh-huh/uh-oh', and function words 'of/from' or commas in transcript-like text.

Function-word token right after a subject or phrase where a predictable continuation follows: contractions "you'll"/"there's", modals ("must", "will"), "%" in "95% CI", and SQL "FROM" after "SELECT *".

retest.explanation: Function-word tokens right after a subject or key term where a predicate/continuation is expected: contraction 'll/'s after you/there, modals (must, will), '%' in '95%' CI, and SQL 'from' after 'select *'.

first.explanation: Separator or connector tokens within a list or parallel pattern (commas, 'one', 'to', '-', '+', 'for') where the next item repeats the structure of earlier items, as in enumerations, ranges like '30 for 30', and operators.

Predicts a verb/adverb right after a clause boundary or subject: imperative "press", negations ("not", "never", "don't"), contrastive "but", plus fragments of split tokens and nested parentheses in math expressions.
Mid-word subword tokens of multi-token place names (Riyadh, Hyderabad, Kolkata, Oman, Shanxi, Uttarakhand) and prefixes like def-/ex-/dep-, plus the noun "role" after a possessive or article.

Whitespace padding runs between columns in markdown/plain-text tables (column gaps), plus the word "more" after a form of "be" (comparative, e.g. "was more pleased"), and similar words like "Stay" or "attention" in prose.

Tokens right after a subject/assignment that predict a following complement: " new" after "var =" in object instantiation code, and motion/posture verbs or prepositions (striding, scurrying, lay on, flopped on, more than) in narrative.

Predictable continuation tokens in code imports/boilerplate (React, {, scala, '.', require) and math-paper phrasing like "can [be] derived/evaluated", where the next token is a highly formulaic, expected word.

Token right after a subject pronoun or relative 'which/who' (I, we, they, he, might), where an adverb or parenthetical comma is inserted before the verb (e.g. 'we, as...', 'I really', 'which specifically', 'might as well').

Second-conjunct connectives in parallel/contrastive structures: 'or', 'nor', 'also' (not only...but also), 'another', and especially repeated 'for' in elliptical parallel clauses (X for A and Y for B), anticipating a repeated structure.
Fires on a split multi-byte token: the broken half of a UTF-8 character (mojibake in Turkish/Chinese text) or a backslash-led LaTeX piece (\ , -\, }\) right before a command name like frac, sigma.

Token right after a list of parallel clauses or a long compound predicate, where the next element needs a verb/auxiliary (was, are, have, could) omitted subject; also the period before a file extension in filenames/URLs and at end of math terms.

Mid-word or mid-token continuation points where the next token is highly predictable: the exponent '3' in 'third derivative of ...**3' math problems, author initial periods in citations, name fragments (Kaczmarek), apostrophes in contractions.

retest.explanation: Mid-word or punctuation tokens in highly formulaic strings: exponent '3' in 'third derivative of ...' math problems, and name/initial fragments (Kacz|mare|k, 'A.' initials, apostrophes) in citations and author lists.

first.explanation: Mid-word subword tokens inside Indian names (e.g. Utt-arak-hand, Mukhe-kar, Ram-ak-rishna), plus sentence-initial "As" in patent text ("As shown in FIG.", "As a result"), where the next token is predictable.

Predicts the next token in highly boilerplate/formulaic text: license headers ("you can redistribute", "You may obtain", "FOR ANY"), Go/C `return` statements, and section-number/DOI fragments like {#sec3dot2-...}.
Token right after a generic subject (noun phrase, 'if', 'a person', 'best') in a general-statement or definition, where a verb/modal like 'is/are/will/to' or pronoun 'you/anyone' is expected next.

Connector word (to, and, by, or, &) linking the first item of a paired or ranged phrase, like 'top to bottom', 'side by side', 'July to September', 'hopes and dreams', predicting the second counterpart.

Boilerplate web/article endings: contact/"for more information, visit" calls to action, URL domain endings, social follow prompts, and disclaimers/declarations ("authors declare that", "no conflict of interest.", "material is"), predicting the next formulaic phrase.

Mid-phrase tokens in scientific/technical text where a physical quantity, substance, or flow is about to be specified, especially temperatures after "at" (at 37 °C), and words like current flowing, ionizing, argon, CO2.

Figure-legend and table-caption boilerplate in scientific papers: the word right after 'shown/represented/indicated' or a visual descriptor (solid, dotted, red, Color, asterisks, ±, 'as', 'by') that precedes a description of plot styling or statistics.

Predicts a verb/word continuation right after a subject or wh-word, especially "are" in "What the hell are...", and mid-word verb stems (assess-es, conduct-s, were-wolf) where a suffix or following word is expected.
Negation words right after an auxiliary or verb (n't, not, no, never), predicting the negated verb or predicate to follow; also weakly opening parentheses in nested arithmetic expressions.

Predicts the next word in memorized boilerplate legal/license text (Apache/BSD licenses, court opinion formulas, funding disclaimers), firing on function words or fixed-phrase tokens like 'Apache', 'permitted', 'in', 'to', and possessive 's'.

Mid-phrase tokens in technical/patent/StackOverflow text where a specific continuation is expected: software version numbers (Ubuntu 14.04, 10.3), '(' after software names, and 'practical', 'need for', 'recommend', 'advantages of'.

Token right after a transitive/action verb that is completing the verb phrase: object pronouns (me, him, us, themselves, it) or adverbs (badly, heavily, intensively, overnight, lightly, once), often just before a prepositional phrase.
Final token of a proper name (surname piece, or company/party name in legal case citations), where the name ends and a delimiter like comma, period, "v.", or title/affiliation follows.

Word right after "play(s) a/an", "had a/an", "have an" etc., where an adjective or modifier is expected (important, crucial, severe, easy), plus mid-word continuations and adverbs like "exponentially".

retest.explanation: Predicts the next word after a verb/article phrase like "plays an [important] role" or "had a [severe]"; fires on adjectives/adverbs or word pieces completing a predictable collocation, especially after "a/an" or "play(s) a".

first.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments (suffix/continuation pieces like -ating, -osing, -ICE) in compound or multi-token words, plus function words like "last"/"the" in "the last", "all the better", where the next token is predictable.

Demonstrative/anaphoric determiners ("this", "that", "such", "these") right after a preposition or verb, referring back to an earlier noun; also mid-identifier tokens (underscores, dots) in code like F_TX_CLOSE macros.

Short structural tokens in formal citations and outlines: list/section markers (a, b, 1, d, iii), legal reporter fragments (App, Civ), name-part or identifier joins (commas, underscores), and abstract-opening "To" after a title.

Function words/prepositions right after a verb or phrase that predicts a specific continuation, like 'start [by]', 'equivalent [to]', 'more [than]', 'by [reducing]'; also the space before citation/reference markers ([@...], \[sec:...]) and mid-word fragments.
Word-fragment tokens in the middle of a word that start with 'or'/'sor'/'tor'/'cor'/'wor' (e.g., Sorbonne, Worcester, torque, corroborated, Toronto), predicting the continuation of the word.
Modifier or possessive token inside a noun phrase (adjective, hyphenated compound part, or 's) where the head noun is expected next, e.g. 'nearby', 'handy', 'Gram-negative', 'Backbone's'.
Fires on the token right after "the/a/of" in a noun phrase, where a head noun or prefix is expected next (e.g. "course of", "sub-", "set of", "half of"); also on code newlines/parentheses.

Mid-word subword fragments inside rare multi-token words/names (Snowdonia, Trafalgar, Congolese, Scuderia), plus predictable function words after passive verbs in methods text (for, into, as) and 'Competing' in 'Competing interests'.

Predictable continuation tokens in structured text: 'endif' after '#' in C preprocessor blocks, closing digits of figure/line IDs (f4, fig4), 'he' after a closing quote in news attributions, and word-completion fragments of names/categories.

Closing or stray punctuation tokens (asterisks, quotes, em-dashes, apostrophes) at emphasis/quote/comment boundaries, often marking where a span ends or interrupts; also 'the' after 'all' in 'all the way'.
Greek-letter prefix tokens (α, β, γ, 'alpha', 'beta') in chemical/biological nomenclature, e.g. α-helix, β-glucan, α-fetoprotein, right before a hyphen; also weakly 'primary' and 'self'.

Fires on the middle or final sub-token of a multi-token proper name, brand, or compound (Joomla, WooCommerce, St John's, National Trust, OpenStreetMap), where the next token completes or follows a known named entity.

The word 'right' (also 'point', 'basis', 'result', 'meaning') as the start of a word or phrase, e.g. 'right hand', 'right-hand side', 'right angles', 'on the basis of', 'as a result', 'point of view'.

Token right after a word that predicts a fixed completion: 'grew [up]', 'for [Defendant]', 'in the [bar]', 'his [mother]/[childhood]', 'for-[each]', 'form_[for]', French 't[-]il'. Predicts a specific next token.
A single lowercase letter token (often d, e, s, v, b, r) in the middle of random alphanumeric strings like hashes, URLs, tweet short links, or IDs, or a word-initial letter after a punctuation mark.
The adverbs/adjectives "long" and "far" (also "Long"/"Far" and the "long" in "longitude"), especially before "-term", "overdue", "run", "list", or "more/from" — extent in time or distance or degree.

Double-newline/blank-line tokens in scraped documents (legal opinions, LaTeX/markdown text) where a paragraph or block break occurs mid-sentence or before an indented equation/list; also fires on mid-token splits (%, �, *).

Word-start fragments and words beginning with "m/mis/min/much/less/far" (much, min, mis-, Miles, Juda-ism, Nishi, -ensa-, -osa-), especially quantity/degree words like "much", "far", "minimum", and subword pieces of such names.

Punctuation or word-fragment tokens that join or introduce a continuation: colons after headline titles, hyphens before clitics (Portuguese -se, -lá), and mid-word pieces like "Del" or "Con" in names and phrases.
Function-like connector tokens mid-sentence after a noun/clause, especially "before", "or", "pour", "+", and the "2" in "So.2d" citations, where the next token continues a phrase or list.

Words right before an expected list of examples or uses/locations: "used [for/as]", "such [as]", "things [like]", "including", "found [along]", "all sorts [of]", typically in descriptive or encyclopedic text, and also indefinite "someone/anyone" fragments.

Element name right after an opening '<' in HTML/XML markup (mostly div, also p, td, li), predicting the attribute or content that follows; also weaker on medical-report words like 'revealed a/an' and color adjectives.

Fires on the word after a verb/"what" where a direct object or complement is expected next: transitive verbs of transfer/cutting (sent, cut, put, set), "what do/does/'s", and possessive 's or underscores.

Predicts a mid-word or mid-phrase continuation token, especially scientific adjectives like "molecular"/"chemical" before weight/mass/shift, plus word-fragment starts (bi-, mo-, F-) and URL slashes or anchor 'f' tokens.

Predicts a repeated or continuing token: the variable in algebra polynomial strings (e.g. "14*y", "- 37*i"), and mid-phrase words like "real", "natural", "general" or name fragments (OpenSC-AD, Adv-ACT) where the next word is highly constrained.

Mid-word subword pieces or final tokens completing multi-token technical/taxonomic terms (Gelechiidae, mahogany, typhimurium, inhibitors), plus paragraph/chapter-break blank lines and year endings; predicts a continuation or suffix.

Word completing a possibility/ability/negation construction, predicting an upcoming infinitive: "no [way]", "little [chance]", "impossible/possible", "unable"; also license-header "Unless" (required by applicable law).

retest.explanation: Words completing negated or modal phrases about possibility/ability, predicting an infinitive: "no [way]", "little [chance]", "not [possible]", "impossible", "unable"; also "Unless" in Apache license headers.

first.explanation: Words denoting history, age or former status in travel-guide descriptions of buildings/places ("former", "past", "Roman", "been" as in 'has been converted', 'artefacts', 'Egyptian' cotton), predicting a historical/heritage description to follow.

Digit tokens inside structured numeric identifiers, especially the middle of UK phone numbers after the area-code hyphen in travel guides, plus case/section/figure numbers and math terms, where the next piece is predictable.

Mid-token continuation inside numbers, hex values, ranges and technical/scientific lists, especially the next digit or fragment of a numeric string (0x4c52, 297449,297578, page ranges 323–366), plus abbreviation/list punctuation.

retest.explanation: Mid-token continuation in structured data: digits/hex after "0x", numeric ranges (page ranges, seqRange coordinates), and list/abbreviation fragments in tables or citations, where the next token is predictable from a pattern.

first.explanation: The token right after the word "For/for" in idiomatic phrases ("for the record", "for all", "for more information", "for completeness"); also fires on word-internal fragments like T-/Sh-ab/ke-b, as in T-shirt, Shabtai, kebabs.

Negation/degree modifiers (non, -, not, less, no, almost, unnecessarily) and coordinating 'and'/citation markers like '@' or '[@' right before an adjective or citation key, predicting the next word in a pair or list.
The contrastive conjunction " but" following a comma after a concession or hedge clause ("I know this is stupid, but..."), anticipating a contrasting clause; weaker on commas and mid-word fragments.
The connector token ("by", "to", "-", "of") inside a repeated or fixed idiom, predicting the repeated word, e.g. "side by side", "time to time", "day-to-day", "know-how", "out of", "all of a sudden".
Preposition/particle following a noun-object in an absolute-style phrase ("guns out", "goal in mind", "interest to uphold", "cash in his pocket"), plus the "R" in "MacRinnalch".

Function words completing a fixed phrase that expects a specific continuation: 'miles north [of]', 'halfway [between]', 'also known [as]', 'arm in [arm]', price ranges '£10 to £[25]', and 'return' statements in code.

retest.explanation: Function words completing a fixed phrase that expects a specific continuation: "miles north [of]", "halfway [between]", "also known [as]", "hand in [hand]", ranges ("£10 to £[25]"), and "return" in code.

first.explanation: Connective function tokens that introduce a following noun phrase, mainly "of" after "one", "Supreme Court" or "population", plus "example"/"instance" in "for example", and "terms" and "due".

Fires on the first token of a modifier or name (often a word fragment like 'My', 'New', 'D', 'electric') right after a determiner/preposition, where a specific noun (term, species, place, technology) is expected next.
Predicts a highly expected, formulaic continuation in fixed phrases or code: 'end result', 'straight games', 'week', 'All-', 'P.J.', 'group_by', 'end', where the next token is strongly predictable.

Mid-word or mid-compound fragments inside multi-word names glued together without spaces: URLs, all-caps identifiers, hyphenated phrases, and macro names, where a name or phrase is still continuing (e.g., www.white|horse, mother-in|-law).

Tokens in the middle of a compound or list where a word was truncated or the apostrophe dropped: possessive nouns missing their apostrophe (players, Marks, dads), and connectors like 'and' or '--' linking figure panels (A and B, A--G).

Connective tokens in lists or boilerplate phrases ("and", "or", commas before the final item, "of", "by") and paragraph-break newlines, where the next word is a predictable continuation of a list or formulaic phrase.

Fires on the token right after a subject noun (often a person/creature) at a verb or particle of approach/arrival (came, approaches, enters, show up), and on mid-word chemical/name fragments like -ic in acids.

retest.explanation: Token right after a subject noun (often a menacing/arriving agent) where a motion verb or particle like came/approached/enters/wander/show up is predicted or occurs; also mid-word fragments like -ic in chemical/names and hyphens.

first.explanation: Predicts a repeated or copied token in a pattern: mainly "of" after container/quantity nouns (cup, pound, volume, rack of), also "'s" in "night's", and repeated identifiers or method names in code/LaTeX.

Mid-phrase tokens in compound or list constructs, especially web/social words (online, Twitter, social media, radio, email) after 'on/a/my', plus mid-word fragments and list commas in code, math and legal text.

Mid-word fragments inside chemical names or rare proper nouns (e.g. 'ethyl', 'methyl', 'Ery', 'ano'), plus operators (+, -) in algebra problems, and code-block newlines/tabs; predicts the continuation of a split word or expression.
The word "least" in the phrase "at least" (before a number or quantity), plus related predicted-continuation tokens like "return/returned" and date month names in formulaic records.
Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is a predictable continuation: 'former' in travel-guide descriptions, word-fragment 'arte(facts)', and list commas or the period after 'for x' in math problems.

Predicts a highly predictable continuation token mid-phrase: adjectives after 'be/is' (available, common, found), '.' after Go package names (types., context.), and case-citation reporter volume digits starting with 9 (9xx F.2d).

Fires on a verb/participle (especially "taken/take/taking") right after an auxiliary or subject, where a passive or phrasal verb is expected (taken a turn, take advantage, been discovered). Also fires on math variables and institution names.

Mid-word subword fragments and function tokens where the next token is a predictable continuation, especially commas ending a fronted descriptive phrase before the main subject (e.g. 'Deep, dark and narrow,' → Loch Ness).
Period after an author's middle/first initial in citations (e.g. "M.G.C.", "J.B.A.") before the surname; also the period in opening hours like "h9.30am". Weaker on comparative "as" and code tokens.

retest.explanation: Period after an initial in author names (e.g. 'M.G.C.' in bibliographies), also the period in opening hours like 'h9.30am'; weaker on 'as'/'was' mid-phrase tokens and code tabs.

first.explanation: Mostly the "MAP" token in Lonely Planet-style travel listings ("(MAP GOOGLE MAP") after a place name and category; also weaker on mid-phrase words in scientific or general text (e.g. "in", "mod", "with") where a noun/complement is expected next.

Verbs of drinking (drinking, sipping, drink) and 'understand/understood', plus 'sense of', 'bottle/glass of', 'fired'; the token right before an expected object or complement, often a beverage or comprehension.

Predicts the next token at a point where a highly predictable continuation follows: closing quote marks ending a dialogue sentence before a paragraph break, or mid-word/boilerplate fragments (e.g., SUBSTITUTE, Appellee, Turkish word pieces).
Predicts a continuation after a short function-like token: indentation after a newline in code, 's after decades/possessives (1970s), 'those'/'that' after 'For'/'But', and the '/' in license URLs.

Mid-word or mid-compound tokens, especially hyphens joining a short capital/prefix to a following word (T-Mobile, D-Wave, Al-Sanadid, 16-bit, X-based), plus split identifiers and numbers where the next piece continues the name.

Function words that open a dependent or modifying phrase and predict a following noun or clause: possessives (her, their, your, whose), "According", "depending", "based", "pursuant", and URL scheme starts (http).

A predicate word or verb right after a subject (esp. "it is/was" or a plural subject) that predicts a following "to"/"that" clause: adjectives like normal, common, rare, fair, easy, or verbs like stop, sit, stand.

Tokens in mid-phrase positions where a continuation is predicted, like commas after a name/date introducing an appositive or relative clause, and fragments inside random hash/ID strings or repeated letter sequences.

Predicts a highly constrained next token in fixed collocations or enumerations: the "of" after nouns like "run/period/series of", "the same", "unusual", labels like panel/step "A", and version-number dots like HTTP/1.1.

retest.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where a highly predictable continuation follows: 'of' after nouns like 'run/series/period/spell', 'same' after 'the', list/enumeration labels (A, B, f), and version-number dots like HTTP/1.1.

first.explanation: Predicts a following object/complement after participles or verbs of drinking/consuming/firing (drinking, smoking, bottle of, glass of), plus mid-sentence continuation tokens like 'as', 'more', and paragraph-break newlines after dialogue.

retest.explanation: Predicts the next word after a mid-sentence participle or clause, especially drinking/firing/smoking verbs ("sat drinking", "firing") and objects like bottle/glass; also fires on paragraph-break newlines after dialogue.

first.explanation: Function/connective words in mid-phrase where a continuation is expected, especially "and" after "how/what/when" ("how and why"), "those" after "For", and "a" in "year and a half"; also some math/LaTeX tokens.

Predicts continuation after a statement-introducing word: copula "is/was" after "The point/thought/question", or verbs like "note/mean/measured", followed by a "that" clause. Also fires on newline after hex constant values and mid-name tokens.

Authorship attribution "by" after titles/'written by' (also author/name starts), and mid-word fragments of proper names or compounds (Zuckerberg, Mendeleev, Suffolk, SourceForge) where the next token is a predictable continuation.

Collective/quantifier nouns after an article or demonstrative that expect "of" next (a [series] of, a [pair] of, this [type]/[class]/[set] of), plus back-references like "above/previous/described" and list or hex-ID fragments.

Sentence-initial "When" starting a temporal clause (often after a paragraph break or quote), plus mid-word "ar" fragments (chaparral, Caernarfon, decarboxylase), and adjectives like "real"/"bigger" after "the".

Mid-word or mid-phrase tokens where the continuation is highly predictable: periods ending equation sentences in synthetic math problems, 'trium' before phal/virate/phant, 'out' after 'watch', and name fragments like 'AR' in Archer.

Function words or word fragments (prepositions like by/to/into/of, 'fact', citation-start spaces) where the next token is a predictable continuation, e.g. a verb-ing, citation marker, or mid-word completion in scientific text.
Predicts continuation after a sentence-ending period in photo captions or inside citation names: "United [States] v.", "F.A[.] Paneth", "U.[S]", and "old" before friend; also dates ending captions.

Predicts a repeated or structurally echoed token: closing-quote-comma after dialogue before a speaker tag, parallel conjunctions/prepositions, repeated words, and URL/code/table delimiters (&, ?, |, http, —).

Predicts a repeated or structured identifier continuation: the token after 'No' (the period) in case/exhibit numbers, plus repeated variable/LaTeX pieces, hyphens in compound terms, and code identifier parts being copied.

Relative pronouns (that/which/who) introducing a relative clause, especially after a coordinating 'and'/'or'; also boilerplate continuations like 'All rights [reserved]', 'Local [Rule]', 'data' availability, and mid-word fragments.

Comma after 'Mon-Sat' in guidebook opening-hours listings, plus other mid-list or parenthetical tokens like numbers after '(' in statistics, 'dad'/'mom' possessives, and continuation points where a sequence will go on.

Predicts the next token after a subject/clause where a verb or connective of consequence/evaluation is expected (made, resulting, giving, seems, should, result); also fires on math/code delimiters like | and +\ inside formulas.

Mid-word subword fragments inside rare or multi-token words (TOURIST, Renovations, Draggables, Rakestraw), plus quantity words like 'one'/'1' after 'at least/exactly', and commas ending introductory clauses.

Word/identifier joints where a compound is split mid-word or at a separator: 'there/here' before -between/-with/-of, 'Never' in 'never mind', and '.' or '_' in package/identifier names like org.apache.commons.math.dist.

Fires on a mid-phrase word or punctuation right after a preposition or clause start, where the next token is highly predictable: 'see [what]', 'in [contrast]', 'the [U].S.', 'at the [beginning]', 'things [people]', and '?' ending question titles.

Predicts a likely next token at mid-phrase function/structural positions: after 'almost' (laughed/smiled), 'No' in docket/case numbers, 'must', 'which', 'affixed', whitespace/newlines in code or legal text, and math-expression variables.
Predicts a pronoun or word completing a comparative or relative clause ("than [I]", "as [you]", "best [I] can"), plus predictable continuation tokens like Klu[wer], "1-[0]", and "if [it]".

Predicts the upcoming verb/clause after an introductory element: mainly the "is" in existential "There is" (also was/comes), and commas ending fronted adverbial or prepositional phrases before the main subject.

Predicts a continuation after a negated or disapproved clause, firing on the word right after a negation or prohibition (not, stop, don't, refuse) or on a conjunction/verb where a negative outcome or verb phrase follows.

retest.explanation: Predicts the next word after a negative/critical or prohibitive context (stop, not, don't, refuse, problematic), mid-clause at points where a verb, conjunction, or complement follows, often describing undesirable actions or flaws.

first.explanation: Predicts a repeated or parallel item in a coordinated structure: commas after list items before 'and', 'the' after 'Both/neither', and repeated tokens in math expressions or LaTeX, anticipating the next parallel element.

Mid-phrase tokens (often pronouns like 'you'/'your', determiners, or a noun) inside instructional or descriptive clauses where a verb or object must follow, e.g. 'the command you [want]', 'a site you [like]', 'near [your] location'.

Token right after a keyword that introduces a new binding or parameter list, where a name or delimiter is expected next: 'Let [x]' in math problems, '|' in block params, '(' after #define macro or function, 'as' in with/except.

retest.explanation: Token right after a binding/definition keyword that introduces a new identifier or parameter list: 'Let' before a variable/function name, 'as' in with/except, lambda/block '|' openers, and '(' after macro or function names.

first.explanation: Mid-text positions where the next token is a predictable repetition or continuation of an earlier phrase, such as a repeated term, matching bracket or closing punctuation, in scientific, code and LaTeX text.

Predicts what follows a short evaluative clause: either the adjective slot in 'it is [common/rare/easy/fair] to/that...' constructions, or the comma before a direct-address name in dialogue ('Nice work, Hawkins').

Verbal-noun/gerund (-ing, -tion, -ment) tokens naming a process or activity (e.g. computing, editing, dephosphorylation, writing, interviewing), often as the subject noun of a clause, predicting a following verb like 'is'/'was' or a head noun.

Token right after a negation or concessive/temporal subordinator (without, not, didn't, even if, although, before he), predicting the continuation of a negated or hypothetical clause, e.g. 'being', 'could', 'not', 'anything'.

Token right after an abbreviation, acronym, or foreign term that introduces its definition or translation: "for", "means", "(", ",", ":", "--" preceding the expansion/gloss (e.g. 'Latin for', 'ACL (', 'SBP,').

Mid-phrase tokens in biographical statements about a person's background or career (e.g. "born and [raised]", "worked as [a]", "grew [up]", "Mr[.]"), predicting the next detail; also operators/symbols in math expressions.

retest.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens in biographical statements ("born and [raised]", "grew [up]", "worked as [a]", "Mr[.]") where a career, upbringing, or personal-history continuation is expected; also fires on math-expression operators.

first.explanation: Enumeration markers introducing list items: the punctuation or newline after 'two reasons/cases/options' announcing a list, and labels like (a), (ii), b, iii, Roman numerals starting a enumerated item or panel.

Function words or tokens right after a subject/time noun that predict a specific continuation: time-offset words ("days later", "next day"), comparison/range prepositions (to, from, for), and "==" in code conditions.

Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is highly constrained by a just-started construction: after verbs/participles (suspended after, picked up, had been), inside split identifiers/words, and sentence-final punctuation in formal text.

Token right after a comparative 'than'/'as' (mostly 'than I'), or a reference numeral/number label (e.g. 'terminal 310', 'Bus 440') — the next item being a short subject pronoun or identifier in technical/numeric text.

Mid-phrase tokens where a continuation is needed: operators (+, -) in algebra word problems, participles/adjectives (restored, converted), 'weather' in 'if the weather's good', and conjunctions/prepositions inside clauses.
Fires at the end of a type/role noun or declaration type token (e.g. 'staffer', 'chelator', 'List<C>', 'Foo *', 'Ref', 'forward'), right before a proper name or variable name is expected.

Fires on the token right after a common function-word or punctuation slot where the next word is highly predictable, e.g. comma after "Yes", "But first", pronoun after "believe", or possessive "his/your/their" before a noun.

Tokens ending an introductory phrase/noun where a subject noun or main clause must follow: commas after fronted modifiers, possessives ('s, its, their), and verb stems, anticipating the head noun or main subject.

Token right after a repeated or previously-mentioned noun/term (spin-wave, MHV RNA, van der Waals, β-cell) or a pronoun/closing quote, where the next word continues a compound or modifies a head noun.
Mid-word subword fragments like "iv", "ir", "av", "ov" inside longer words (convivial, Oblivion, reactivate, captivating, festival), where the vowel+v/r piece sits in the middle of a word.

Predicts a continuation after a mid-phrase word, mostly transitive verbs or prepositions that await an object (admit, recognize, heard, account, to, for), plus opening brackets and colons introducing code or an example.
Mid-word subword fragments, especially "eps", "ots", "ps", "ars", "aps" inside split words/names (Botswana, Cotswolds, dyspepsia, 'eps-matches'), plus "out" after verbs and LaTeX "{\" tokens.

retest.explanation: Mid-word subword fragments such as 'eps', 'ots', 'ps', 'ars', 'am' (Botswana, Cotswolds, dyspepsia, 'eps-matches'), plus 'out' after verbs (pull out, get it out there) and LaTeX '{\'.

first.explanation: Tokens right after a variable/property name that predict an upcoming value or object, mainly the assignment "=" in code (var x =), plus "help" in "can someone help me" and adverbs like "independently", "watch".

Mid-word or mid-name fragments, especially after initials or in the middle of names and hyphenated compounds (D.P[.], Dan P[oul]ter, high through[-]put, USE_[AT]OMIC), where the next token is a continuation.

Mid-phrase function/connector tokens or separators (of, We, /, ,, -) where the next token is a continuation, often following numbers or digits like 5; common in scientific/chemical names and technical text.

Word-start tokens like "Bill", "May", "Sam", "William", "count", "shall", "can" — especially the name Bill (also as fragment in billboard/billow/billings) — where the token could begin a longer word or be a name/word ambiguity.

retest.explanation: Tokens that are names or word-pieces like "Bill" (esp. the person's first name, or inside billboard/billow/Billings), plus similar fragments: May/may, Sam, William, count, shall, which begin other words or names.

first.explanation: Mainly the word "you" after "Thank" (also "Thanks" openers) in thank-you replies; weaker on "Oh,", statistical phrasing (p-value, indicated), and the hyphen in scientific notation like e-10.
The word right after a partitive quantifier like "some", "much", "most", "a lot", or "majority", especially the "of" or "the" in "some of the…" / "most of the…", predicting a following noun phrase.

Mid-sentence tokens where a clause could end or continue: sentence-final periods/closing parens after a complete statement, plus verbs/connectives (put, lodged, found, introduce) predicting the next word. Also mid-word fragments like 'oc'.

Predicts the next token in synthetic math-problem and structured code text: the number after "Is/Does" in divisibility questions, the "h" of "i'th term", closing parentheses in function definitions, and tabs or newlines in repetitive lists.

retest.explanation: Predictable structural tokens in synthetic math problems (e.g. 'Is [5] a factor', 'i't[h] term', closing parens in function definitions) and repeated-pattern code/list lines; fires where the next token follows a templated format.

first.explanation: Predicts an upcoming pronoun (it/them/they) referring back to a just-mentioned subject; fires on prepositions, 'that', 'because', or punctuation right before the pronoun, e.g. 'has a nice heft to [it]', 'in that [it]', 'brought with [it]'.

Mid-word or mid-compound continuation tokens: suffixes, hyphens, possessive 's, or fragments of names and citations (e.g. Bank-Illinois, cousin's, P.3d), where the next token continues an ongoing multi-part name or phrase.

Legal citation internals: closing parenthesis after a year, or final digits of page/pin-cite numbers in case reporters (F.2d, U.S., P.2d); also weakly digits in math strings and mid-phrase function words.

Industry/domain noun or hyphen/abbreviation used as the first element of a compound or noun phrase (music, game, law, security, energy, app, book-, Elec.) where the next token continues the compound, e.g. 'music business', 'law enforcement'.
Tokens right after an instrumental 'with'/'using'/'use' that introduce the tool or means of an action (e.g. 'with [his] finger', 'using [a]', 'used [the]'), predicting the instrument noun next.

retest.explanation: Token right after an instrumental 'with'/'using'/'use' (or 'used'), predicting the tool or instrument being employed next, typically a determiner/possessive like 'a', 'his', 'her', or the word 'using' itself.

first.explanation: Fires mid-phrase on the word "by" (also "read", "receive", "request") where a fixed idiom or compound is expected, e.g. "by-product", "by reputation", "day by day", and on standalone numbers/line breaks.

Connector tokens inside lists or ranges (hyphen/en dash in day or page ranges like Sun-Thu or 261–266, commas in index page lists, 'and'/'&' joining paired items), where the next item is expected to follow.
Sentence-start connectives and function words that predict a continuation, like "Therefore", "Conversely", "However", "Yeah"/"Yes" answers, and "the"/"why", plus syntax tokens in code and LaTeX.
Newline/blank-line tokens after short heading or title lines (section headers in scraped web text), plus the word 'analy-' forms (analyse, analytical) and scattered tokens in code or citations.

Predicts the next token at highly formulaic mid-pattern positions in structured text: code/markup syntax (type=", <, =>), legal citation numbers (S.Ct. 72), and scientific units/concentrations (0.01 M, toluene).

Predicts a repeated or highly predictable continuation token: copying an identifier from earlier context (e.g. 'pone' in PLOS ONE refs, '475' in ISSN, repeated numbers) or a common next word (I, just, CI, Pacific).

Fires on the head token of a physical quantity or variable (T, s, r, f, energy, frequency, sensitivity, ability) in scientific/LaTeX text, where a threshold, range, or inequality or 'of/to' complement is expected next.

Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is a predictable completion: quantifier/comparative idioms (at most/least, far exceed, fine), opening quotes in dialogue, digits in arithmetic sequences, and ampersand/'and' in names.

Punctuation or list markers right after an announced enumeration ("two reasons/options/methods"), predicting the items to follow: the period/colon ending the intro sentence, or "(ii)", "one [of]", "most" in list enumerations.

The exponent operator "**" in polynomial expressions of synthetic math problems (e.g. "Let f(x) be the derivative of x**4/4 + 10*x**3/3"); weaker on mid-word/compound continuation tokens like gamma-ray, Zariski, and "10" in IDs.

Mid-word or mid-phrase tokens predicting a continuation: especially "obsess(ive)", "adren(aline)", year/time expressions ("-" in 2014-15, "years", "decade", "year"), category year labels ("Category:1978"), and name fragments.

Predicts a highly formulaic continuation token inside boilerplate or multi-token identifiers, e.g. "(at) your option" in GPL text, "call-template", "Return to text", and mid-word or underscore pieces.

Word-continuation tokens after an initial 'F'/'f' fragment, where a word or name starting with F is split into subword pieces (e.g. F|ais|al, F|fest|iniog, F|ult|on, f|ath|oming); also nearby 'fail/free/full'.
Fires on the word-start fragment " Se"/"SE" (also "E", "HE", "Y") as a token beginning a word or name, e.g. Seçmen, Señorías, Seahawks, SECONDS; strongest after "Toplam" in Turkish election tables.

Tokens inside a conditional or comparison expression just before the comparison/predicate continues (e.g. `if (j <`, `x ===`, `& 0x7) !=`, `if forgn is`), mostly in code, plus similar mid-clause positions in prose.

Mid-word subword fragments or mid-expression tokens where the continuation is highly predictable: split rare words (irrep-ress-ible, e-leg-ans, anach-ronism), LaTeX/number syntax pieces, and "even/to/as" in fixed phrases.

Fires on structural/formatting tokens in the middle of a pattern: blank lines before section headings (External links, References), citation page-range digits, footnote markers like [^], hyphens in citation syntax, and mid-word fragments.
Word right after a sentence-initial "In" in fixed phrases ("In any case/event", "In other words", "In the..."), also "in" before seasons/months; weaker on mid-name tokens like Sar-ap-en, S-amp-els.

Tokens completing a distance/time expression in travel-guide directions ("half a mile", "10 minutes' walk", "1.5 miles east"), plus similar predictable continuation tokens like "Circuit Judge" and math/code syntax.

Predicts the next structural token in scientific/web boilerplate, especially the number inside table/figure reference links like "(Table [3](#Tab3){ref-type", plus newlines after share/like lines and mid-phrase tokens.

Interjections like "Ah/Oh/Uh/Hmm" (often elongated, e.g. "Uh-huh", "Ahh") starting an utterance, and the noun right after the indefinite article "a" in appositive descriptions ("a peninsula", "a genus").

Mid-construct tokens where the next token is a predictable continuation: code identifiers (get/return/current), operators like '=' or '*', whitespace padding in tables, and idiom words (a kick, both times).

Word pieces like lead/leading, delay(ed), active/reactive/responsive, response, driving, sensitive, PE, send/transmit: dynamic process or causation words, often as the first part of a compound or modifier before a noun.

retest.explanation: Word-start fragments like lead/leading, delay(ed), driv(ing), respons(e/ive), react(ive)/active, sensitive, PE — mainly adjectival or modifier tokens (delayed diagnosis, leading actress, reactive oxygen) that precede or begin a noun phrase.

first.explanation: Fires on a token in the middle of a construct where a specific kind of continuation is strongly expected: articles/adjectives before a noun ("a", "an", "all"), or code syntax like ":", ":=", "!", "join", "define" before a type or argument.

Token right after a verb/phrase where the object or completion is expected next, especially pronoun "me/them" after verbs like trust, bear with, listen to, stay with; also "=" in variable assignments in code.

Predicts a main verb or following word right after a subject noun/relative pronoun (e.g. 'that [owns/stores/provide]', 'Payton [said]', 'told'), plus mid-sequence tokens in lists and numbers; focuses on what comes next.

Fires on the token right after a start-of-utterance or mid-expression position: variable in math polynomial definitions (e.g. '*m**2'), first token of dialogue replies ('Yeah', 'Ex'cuse), Japanese subtitle starts, and verbs like 'require'.

Mid-word or mid-structure tokens where the next piece is highly predictable continuation: split-word fragments (Her-p-az, out-p-acing), hyphens in names (HIM-6), numeric table cells and closing parentheses, and function words after verbs (do it, must be).

Word right after "I am/I'm/get/have/need" in phrases about a person's state or possessions, especially "I am [new] to..." (beginner/newbie) and "get/have [your/my/their] ..." (possessive pronoun), anticipating a noun or "to".

Tokens in the middle of a phrase where a predictable continuation follows: prepositions after 'fall/border/verge' (within, into, on), numbers within sequences, and words like 'as' before 'above' or 'is' predicting what comes next.

Tokens ending a short phrase just before a likely closing/continuation, esp. parenthetical hedges like "if [any]", "in [part]", hesitation fillers (Um, Uh), and measurement unit tokens (mm, ppm) after numbers.

Predictable continuation tokens in structured text: the minus after 'return' in C error codes (-ENOMEM, -EINVAL), '=' or '+' operators after identifiers, list commas, 'you' after 'How are', and newline/indent tokens in repetitive lists.

Predicts the next token in rigidly patterned or structured text: mid-word fragments of names, the 'mutations=' field in cigar strings, dialogue speech verbs after quotes (pleaded, sighed), LaTeX/code continuations and number digits.

Tokens in the middle of a word or structure where the next token is a predictable continuation: subject pronouns after 'what/if/whether/knew' (I, he), mid-word fragments of rare names, and code/LaTeX delimiters like ';' or ','.

Mid-phrase tokens in paired or comparative constructions (X and/or Y, input/output, more than, much more than we), where the next word must mirror an earlier term (e.g., 'and' joining parallel nouns, 'than we export').

Function-word or structural tokens at a boundary where a continuation is expected: sentence-initial "As" and "as" after verbs like 'used'/'acts', plus newlines after closing braces in code and XSL 'otherwise' tags.
Mid-expression tokens in math/code/technical text where the next token is a predictable continuation: LaTeX braces after \frac, operators, brackets, numbers, or nouns like 'system', 'samples', 'of'.

Predicts continuation of structured or repetitive sequences: list separators in index/number lists, blank-line or indentation tokens in PHP code, and mid-word fragments (succ-um-bed, Thess-al-onica); fires on the delimiter or fragment token.

Mid-phrase tokens where the next word is highly predictable: idiomatic distance/time phrases (not too far [off], days fly [by], far [away]), blank-line breaks in poems/lyrics, and code format-string or literal tokens like ("\ and 1.

Function words or punctuation at mid-sentence points where a continuation is highly predictable (e.g., 'in' before a case name, 'the' in 'the X-er the Y-er', legal citations, paragraph-break newlines); a syntactic-slot predictor, most common in legal text.

Predicts the next token in a highly formulaic citation or notation pattern: the period in legal reporter cites like 'F.2d', 'et' before 'al.', '&' in names, exponent digits like '^−1^'; also some filler words.
Mid-word fragments of rare names/technical terms (K-oc-henberger, Gaug-uin), plus 'the court' subject tokens in legal text, and newline after image captions/credits; predicts a continuation token.

Mid-token predicting a continuation after an abbreviation/partial word: mostly the period in legal footnote citations ("n." before a number), plus "like"/"of" and word-fragment tokens in the middle of compounds.

Mid-word fragments and quantifier/preposition tokens after verbs of feeling, plus affectionate 'sweet'/'love' terms (sweetie, Luv) and random-string/ID pieces; fires where a following noun or word continuation is expected.

Tokens right before "first" in "for the first time" / "this is the first study/report" novelty claims (mostly "the", "for", "reported"); also a weaker firing on capital "E" starting names or acronyms.

Mid-sentence word right after a noun or verb phrase that expects a continuation, often a participle, preposition, or complementizer (made, derived, constructed, if, that, of, want), anticipating what follows. Also 'previous/above [Lemma/theorem]'.

Fires on a word in a highly predictable fixed phrase or idiom, where the token continues a collocation (e.g. 'beyond a reasonable doubt', 'bursting at the seams', 'inspired', 'Bus 118' in transit listings).

Predicts a following quantity/object after a transitive verb or connector: 'any' after verbs/prepositions (met any burden, REPLACE any), and 'to/and/than/,' in numeric ranges or comparisons (4GB to 8GB, 25 and 35).

retest.explanation: Mid-phrase tokens where a following quantity, noun, or number is predicted, especially the determiner "any" after a verb or preposition ("met any burden"), plus "to/and/than" in numeric ranges and comparisons.

first.explanation: Mid-word or mid-compound continuation tokens (hyphens, syllable fragments, punctuation, function words) where the next piece is a predictable continuation, e.g. pronunciation guides, name fragments, identifiers, LaTeX/code separators, and phrasal 'of/or/to'.

retest.explanation: Mid-word or mid-compound continuation tokens (hyphens, fragments, particles) where the next piece is a predictable completion, e.g. pronunciation hyphens, name pieces like At|ch|afalaya, 'out of', 'GSM-based', code identifiers.

first.explanation: Mid-token positions where the next token is highly predictable continuation: operators/digits in algebra exercises (e.g., '2[[*]]c**2'), decimals in stats tables, LaTeX fragments, split words/emails (inter|pelado, dr.), and prepositions in fixed phrases.

Predictive mid-pattern tokens in formulaic text: legal citations (reporter volume numbers, commas after case names), date day-numbers after month, assignment operators in code, and mid-word fragments, where the next token is highly predictable.

retest.explanation: Mid-structure tokens in predictable formulaic text: legal citation pieces (volume numbers, commas after case names), date day numbers, code assignment operators, and mid-word fragments, where the next token is highly predictable.

first.explanation: Predicts an upcoming boolean/enumerated value or count: fires on assignment operators before true/false (flag = true), and on 'There are two/at least' phrases introducing forms, varieties or species.

Fires on the word after an infinitive 'to' or a 'to which' construction, where a verb or complement of a stranded/fronted clause is expected (e.g. 'to dry', 'introduce themselves', 'enough to'); also some code and LaTeX tokens.

Predicts the next token mid-phrase at a point where a continuation is expected: verbs/function words after a subject or auxiliary in legal prose, '.' before method names (System.out.), and '0' before 'x' in hex constants.

Predicts a continuation after a coordinated list item or comparative clause: commas/"and"/"or" in lists of verbs or adjectives, and auxiliaries/predicates after "as ... as they/it" or "the only difference" constructions.

Predicts what follows the word "life" (or similar subjects like career, reign) — fires on "life" itself and on the next token ("was", "has"), especially in phrases like "his life was in danger", "life-threatening", and "ground to a halt".

Mid-phrase function words or word fragments where the next token is a highly predictable continuation, especially "and [so] on/forth", plus subword pieces (Sp-, Fer-, Emb-) and connectors like "of", "need", "why".

Sentence-ending newlines/periods (end of a sentence or paragraph, before a new line), plus mid-sentence positions after an adverb/adjective or verb where a complement is expected (e.g. 'sufficiently', 'accurately').

Mid-phrase tokens in scientific/technical text where a predictable continuation follows: hyphens after durations (6-month, 24-hour), 'This' opening study descriptions, 'Short' in medical names, and split code identifiers (CreatePreparer).

Section-heading and formal-document structure tokens in legal/scientific text (ANALYSIS, CONCLUSION, Proof, 'Upon review/consideration', 'following'), where the next token is a newline or the section body begins.

Predicts a continuation in an enumerated or parallel series: sentence-initial rhetorical "Why" after a comma/period, list markers like " (" before iv/C, numbered line starts, "Hall-ib-urton" fragments, and repeated sequence/citation tokens.

retest.explanation: Sentence-initial or clause-initial rhetorical "Why"/"what"/"who" after a comma or period ("Well, why..."), plus list/enumeration markers like " (" before (ii)/(iv), "ib" in Halliburton, and numbering whitespace tokens in lists.

first.explanation: Fires at points where the next token is a predictable continuation: mid-word fragments of names and identifiers (Goebbels, Analyzer), sentence-final punctuation after 'he said', and words like 'own', 'only', 'who'.

Mid-phrase function/connector tokens that expect a continuation: prepositions/particles after verbs (back, behind, inside, over, off), 'of' after 'one', 'and', plus newlines after code closing braces and colons or hex digits in code.

Tokens that begin a short fragment where the next token is highly predictable: exponent carets (^) in LaTeX math like χ^2, the verb 'seek/sought', 'Such a', and mid-word pieces or long whitespace-indentation in code.

retest.explanation: Mid-word or syntax fragments predicting a continuation: superscript/subscript markers (^, _, ^{) in LaTeX math, forms of 'seek/sought/such/trying', and whitespace-padded code alignment tokens.

first.explanation: Fires on the word after a hyphen/compound or subject noun where a repeated or paired term is expected (e.g. one-on-[one], client-to-[client], Soviet [Union], 'processing [were]'), predicting the continuing word or verb.
Token right after a verb of dying/killing (died, killed, perished) predicting the next word, e.g. 'died [from/in/on/while]'; also fires on mid-word or next-token positions in prose and code.

Mid-clause tokens where the next word is a predicted continuation about a cost, burden, or requirement (e.g. reduce, required, more, space, have to), especially in problem/disadvantage contexts; also clause-boundary words and punctuation.

Plural category nouns (or list/index tokens) that head a set of examples, predicting a following "like/such as/including" or "here and there" enumeration, e.g. "TV shows like", "Famous students", "x_1".

Syntactic junctures in expository prose where a clause or phrase continues: sentence-ending periods, commas, conjunctions (and/or/but), auxiliary verbs, and paragraph breaks, predicting what follows next, plus mid-word fragments.

Tokens where the next word is highly predictable from structure: closing brackets/braces in LaTeX, repeated variables in algebra simplification, and unit nouns after 'per half/full' (day), or noun-phrase heads in set phrases.

Fires on highly predictable boilerplate/formulaic continuation tokens, where the next word is strongly determined: license text ('License for'), sentence-ending periods, mid-phrase words like 'Eagle', 'xsl:', 'Purch|aser', 'entit|les'.

Citation/attribution and cross-reference slots: the word right after "As [Author]" (writes, notes, explains, words), "discussed/described [in/below]", or inside citation numbers and closing quotes, where a source or referenced passage comes next.

Predicts upcoming "first"/"only"/ordinal words: fires on determiners or prepositions in phrases like "this is [the] first study", "for [the] first time", "not [the] first time", "between [any] two", "all [but] one".

Verbs/words about funding, paying, or allocating money/resources (funded, financed, split, spread, allocated, distributed, diverted, proceeds will), especially predicting the next word like 'by', 'to', or the money recipient/purpose.

Token right after a wish/desire/need construction, predicting a hypothetical or desired clause: mainly the subject after "wish" ("I wish [I]"), also "need [for]", "call [for]", "better [way]", "there had to [be]".

Mid-construction tokens in degree/extent or range phrases where a continuation is expected: the "so [much/good/big]" before "that/so", "to the point/extent", and range connectors like "from X [to] Y", "as low as".

Function words or modal/auxiliary tokens right after a subject or noun phrase, where a predicate or verb phrase is expected next (e.g. 'will', 'should', 'be', 'might', 'of', 'doubt[less]'), predicting what follows.

Predicts the verb or auxiliary after a subject in legal/judicial or directive statements ("must", "should", "will", "be"), e.g. "judgment must be reversed", and the comma after "Accordingly" in court rulings.

Tokens right before a numeric value or quantity is stated, especially after a change/comparison verb (increased by, at least, on the order of, to a lesser extent, equal to), or an assignment/colon before a value.

Mid-token fragments in structured or scraped text: markdown table separator dashes, citation/reference IDs (e.g. @gks1234-B, 1471-2164-14-505), figure filenames, and numeric delimiters; also occasionally 'diverse' or 's.

Mid-expression tokens where the next token is highly predictable from a pattern: operands/variables in synthetic algebra and arithmetic problems (numbers, x, n, closing parens), plus completions of multi-token names or phrases.

Mid-phrase function words/punctuation in stock or idiomatic expressions where a specific continuation is highly predictable (e.g., 'none of your business', 'opinions expressed... sole responsibility', 'make sure', 'please see', 'use the').

Predicts the next token in contexts where a pair/duality was set up (two, both, one of, first of two) or a subscript index follows; fires on structural tokens like underscores, commas, 'is', 'the' before the second element.

Verbs or prepositions right after a subject, predicting a location/path complement: especially buses/lines 'stop', 'pass', 'come' through/in a place (travel-guide transit phrasing), and motion/position words before 'to/in/at/through'.
